title: Even God wants a blessing (Berakhot 7a)
hookLine: the high priest Ishmael is asked by God for a blessing, and blesses God with mercy
tomorrow: where does God live when the Temple is gone?

cards: A whiff of cinnamon, and you're back in somebody's kitchen years ago, before you've even placed it.
Berakhot's next story begins inside a cloud of smell: incense, in the innermost room of the Temple, where a priest has come in alone. And in that smoke, God asks him for a blessing.

teach.b: Rabbi Ishmael son of Elisha tells it himself. Once I went into the innermost sanctum to offer incense, and I saw Akatriel Yah, the LORD of hosts, seated on a high and lifted throne.
And He said to me: Ishmael, My son, bless Me. Stop there. The LORD of hosts asks a human being for a blessing.

teach.h: MAY YOUR MERCY CONQUER YOUR ANGER.
teach.b: He gives back yesterday's prayer: may it be Your will that Your mercy conquer Your anger, that Your mercy prevail over Your other ways, that You deal with Your children with mercy, beyond the letter of the law.
And God nodded His head to him. A nod, in the smoke.
Then the Talmud draws the lesson: don't let the blessing of an ordinary person be light in your eyes. If God wanted Ishmael's, an ordinary blessing counts.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: in the Talmud, God asks a priest for a blessing, and answers it with a nod. So blessing doesn't only flow down, from the great to the small. It can rise.
A child can bless a parent, a student a teacher, a person God.

how: Many Jewish parents bless their children on Friday night, and when someone says a blessing aloud, those who hear it answer amen.

games.q: what does “even god wants a blessing” mean?
o: a blessing said over wine before a festival meal
the priests' blessing given to the people each day
God asks a person for a blessing, and receives one

games.q: the incense and the blessing — tap the pairs.
p: asks: Ishmael, My son, bless Me
may Your mercy conquer Your anger

s: in Jewish tradition, blessings only flow from the greater to the lesser
in Berakhot 7a God asks a priest for a blessing, and nods when it comes.
the Talmud's lesson: don't take an ordinary person's blessing lightly
if God wanted Ishmael's blessing, an ordinary blessing counts.
Ishmael blesses God with mercy, beyond the letter of the law
his words echo God's own prayer from the same page.

games.q: your teacher has had a rough week, and the class is quiet. you want to say something kind, but she's the teacher. what does Berakhot 7a suggest?
o: say it; an ordinary person's blessing isn't light, even to someone above you.
leave it; encouragement should come from those above, not from below.
wait until she asks for it, the way God asked Ishmael first.
games.why: the Talmud's own lesson from the story: don't let an ordinary person's blessing be light in your eyes. it can rise.

practice: If there's a spice jar, a tea bag or a candle within reach, hold it close and breathe in slowly; if not, call up the smell of something warm. Let the scent bring you to one person above you, a parent, a teacher, a boss, an elder.
For the rest of the sit, wish them one good thing, in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Even God wants a blessing. Rabbi Ishmael, asked by God to bless, blesses God with mercy, and God nods.

orig.note: Hebrew: Ishmael, My son, bless Me, God's words in Berakhot 7a.

carryVoice: Something to keep: bless the one above, and never call a small blessing light. Berakhot, day eight.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 7a (Rabbi Ishmael son of Elisha: the incense, Akatriel Yah, 'Ishmael, My son, bless Me'; the blessing of mercy; God nods; don't take an ordinary person's blessing lightly)
